parsed.explanation: The dominant traveller-facing exposure is the entry gate: sex is redefined as birth-assigned for documents, X markers are no longer processed, and officers are instructed to refuse cases where records cast doubt on an applicant's sex, with a possible lifetime fraud finding. Foreign governments have issued advisories and detentions of trans travellers are reported. Inside the country, exposure is uneven: facility bans in many divisions (four criminalising in some circumstances, one arrest documented) and a division ban extended to colleges in 2026, plus documented harm in immigration and prison custody (hormone removal, forced labour, assault). Countervailing: no criminalisation of trans identity, a national gender-identity hate-crime statute, working courts that have enjoined several orders, and wide safe-division variance. The border chain, not everyday street life, sets the score: materially below the 0.55 anchors, above the criminalising 0.15 tier.

entry_documents.exposure: Sex defined as birth-assigned for national documents; X markers no longer issued; officers instructed to refuse where documents or records cast reasonable doubt on sex, and suspected misrepresentation of sex may support permanent lifetime inadmissibility; passports reportedly confiscated, travellers stranded; at least eight governments issued advisories after detentions of foreign nationals.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiry; fraud finding requires all four elements, is never automatic and has limited waivers; litigation by a civil-liberties union continues; legal-aid FAQ on document rules.
entry_documents.interaction: Marker/appearance mismatch at a port of entry → secondary screening → discretionary refusal or detention, feeding directly into immigration custody; home-country documents are judged by national adjudicators.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Immigration custody: trans men report forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse. National corrections policies from 2026 mandate haircutting, hormone removal and psychiatric substitution; the division operates a 'freeze-frame' restriction on inmate treatments; trans prisoner counts no longer reported.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Gender identity covered by the national hate-crimes statute; several executive orders enjoined in court; no division rule on cell placement or segregation recorded either way.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A border refusal escalates into the immigration-custody system where the documented abuse occurs; the division's treatment restriction compounds exposure for anyone held locally.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National order bars trans people from federally funded single-sex facilities matching identity. Division law (enacted 2024, extended 15 May 2026) requires students in public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching birth sex; one arrest documented — handcuffed, 24 hours in a men's ward, trespass charge.
federal_state_facilities.protection: The division law is unenforceable against one plaintiff while appellate litigation proceeds; 29 divisions plus four units and the capital district have no mapped ban; the division's statute requires willful entry plus refusal to depart, not automatic arrest.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Facilities are governed by division and building-level rules layered on the national funding condition; a visitor entering a public campus building faces division enforcement, not national.

care_services.exposure: National order frames minor gender-affirming care as mutilation; proposed rules would bar public reimbursement under 18; care banned in 27 divisions; inmate care denial documented.
care_services.protection: No visitor-facing care-denial rule documented; several measures enjoined.
care_services.interaction: A travelling family with a trans minor could hit reimbursement and prescribing gaps; adult visitor emergency care exposure is not documented.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: May 2026 counterterrorism strategy prioritises 'neutralization' of groups described as 'radically pro-transgender'; a justice-department reward memorandum invokes 'radical gender ideology'; orders direct investigation of schools facilitating social transition and rescind pronoun policies.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: The strategy states counterterrorism powers will not target mere disagreement; courts have blocked multiple orders; national hate-crime coverage exists.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Raises risk chiefly for visibly activist travellers or those whose devices/online content are examined at the border, not for ordinary tourist conduct.

minors_guardians.exposure: Division school-facility mandate reaches K-12; national orders target teachers who use preferred names; care restrictions for minors in 27 divisions.
minors_guardians.protection: Injunctions against several orders; no documented enforcement against a visiting family.
minors_guardians.interaction: Short-stay visitors rarely enrol, but a guardian travelling with a visibly trans minor inherits the same border document exposure.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Division has no hate-crime statute (absence confirmed since 2007); 37 divisions lacked gender-identity bias statutes as of 2019; 66% poll support for birth-sex document rules signals disapproval.
street_violence_police_response.protection: National gender-identity hate-crime statute; 22 divisions plus the capital district bar gender-identity discrimination; no documented pattern of trans-specific street violence against visitors.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Disapproval is expressed politically rather than through documented visitor-targeted violence; local police response to a trans visitor's complaint is undocumented.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Appeals go to the same agencies; passport policy still in litigation; a refused traveller may be stranded before any remedy is reached.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Civil-liberties suit, injunctions, appellate orders (including one requiring a school district to accommodate a trans student), legal-aid guidance.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Courts work but slowly and after the harm; remedy does not restore a missed trip or reverse a border refusal in real time.

anchor_checks.comparison: Similar in kind — border officers empowered to refuse trans travellers with no effective appeal — but this jurisdiction adds a potential lifetime fraud finding, documented detentions of foreign nationals, and a custody system with reported abuse, making the post-refusal trajectory worse. It scores slightly below 0.35-A despite lacking a formal morality register.

Kestrel Isles limits harms to administrative refusal and return transport with an appeal desk. Here refusal can escalate into immigration detention with documented forced labour and sexual abuse, plus criminal facility exposure in some divisions. Materially worse than 0.55-B.

Meridia trains border officers and provides tribunal review, counsel and compensation for unlawful holding. This jurisdiction offers litigation after the fact but no operative on-the-spot remedy, and its facilities and custody records are hostile. Well below 0.75-C.

Varnalia's harm is recurring police raids, fines and extortion, with imprisonment rare. Here there is no street-level targeting or extortion, but the border chain and custody conditions carry higher severity. Slightly above 0.25-A, not a tier above.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime is a functioning, litigious state enforcing a hostile documentary and facilities posture. The traveller meets it first at the border: a marker or appearance mismatch triggers instructed refusal, possible lifetime inadmissibility, and detention that feeds a custody system with documented hormone removal, forced labour and assault. In-country exposure is uneven — facility bans bite mainly in public buildings and, in this division, on campuses — while ordinary tourist life carries no documented targeting. Courts enjoin orders and hear challenges, but only after the traveller has been refused, stranded or held. The border chain and its custody tail, not street life, fix the rating.
